entries.answer: A website in Filipino is a website, pronounced with a w and not the Filipino v, and it is the most common way to refer to a page or a site online. The word covers two sizes that English keeps separate: a single page, which most Filipinos call a website, and a whole collection of pages under one name, which is also a website. A specific page within a site is often called a link, meaning the address, so a person asking you to send the link usually means the whole site rather than one page inside it. The related words follow the same borrowing pattern, and a Filipino speaker will say a webpage or a site without hesitation. The practical difference between a website and the app on a phone is that one is addressed on a browser and the other is installed, and a person who says may app ako usually means the installed kind even though a website can now do much the same job.

patterns: is wifi the same as internet
entries.answer: Wifi is the short form of the marketing term wireless fidelity, but the full form is not what it means: there is no agreed standard for fidelity, and the term was created partly because the longer phrase could not be trademarked. What wifi actually describes is a set of standards for sending data over radio without wires, the oldest still in use being the family the mark is normally understood to mean, plus the newer faster versions most phones now use. The practical things a user needs to know are about the band and the distance: a 2.4 gigahertz band reaches further and passes through walls better but is crowded, a 5 gigahertz band is faster and shorter range, and being close to the router matters more than the number on the box. In the Philippines, household wifi is often a shared connection whose cost is split, and the practical complaint is contention rather than the line itself: when everyone in the building is watching video at once, the same connection slows down for all of them.
